label: MiniMax M3.1 Flash
output:
Peter, thanks for laying that out. You're the only person here who's actually run payroll for nine years, and that's precisely why your cash-flow argument is the one I take most seriously rather than the one I push back on. The point about recovery from leavers is fair. The "one month ahead permanently" point is fair, and I'd say you were right about it in our case.

But we've run your version of this, and I'd like to put the numbers somewhere Brenda can use on the 18th.

**We closed our window in February 2025**

The internal pushback was, almost word for word, the argument you make: we are not a bank, the forecast breaks, some people take an advance every month, HR becomes the lender of first resort. We gave two months' notice and ran one financial literacy session with the SACCO. Nobody argued with the principle.

Six months after closing, debt collector and loan app calls to our office went from a handful to **61 logged by reception**. That's reception's log, not a survey — calls received and noted. Several of the apps had our supervisors listed as "referees" and were ringing their personal numbers asking about employment and salary level.

The part that isn't a number is the number that matters: unplanned absence on the two days after month-end rose. Our fleet manager tied at least three missed Mombasa runs to drivers who were "sorting out loans" when they were rostered to be on the road.

The shift didn't stop the borrowing. It moved it from a payroll deduction we could see to six loan apps at once at interest we don't control. One loader at Changamwe came to me with six apps running simultaneously, borrowing from one to pay the other. It took us four months with payroll to unwind that. That's what "they always adjust" looks like from inside the depot.

**What we reopened in September 2025, and how it's performing**

Written policy, not an informal practice:

- Maximum **40% of net pay**
- Once per pay cycle
- Repaid in full at the next payroll, no fee
- Requested through the payroll portal, not through my office
- We check the request against the Employment Act limit on deductions (two-thirds of wages) before approving, so nobody ends up with nothing at month end

The numbers since reopening:

- **55–70 requests a month**, averaging around **KES 9,000**
- **Recovered 100%**, except two leavers
- **Total written off for the year: roughly KES 14,000**

Our people net around KES 28,000 a month, so the 40% ceiling works out to about KES 11,200. The average request is KES 9,000. The gap between those two figures is the answer to your concern about people taking it every month and taking too much: the cap does that work, not a closed window.

**Your four arguments, one at a time**

*The company shouldn't be in that business.* Agreed in principle, which is why the cap is hard. If a request is more than 40% of net, it doesn't come to us — it goes to the SACCO or nowhere. Our exposure is bounded and predictable.

*Every hour spent approving advances is an hour not spent on HR.* Also fair, and it's why we moved the intake to the payroll portal. HR no longer adjudicates emergencies. Payroll approves against a written rule. It's a rule applied consistently rather than a favour I grant or refuse depending on who walks in.

*Good luck recovering it when someone leaves.* With a written policy and recovery at the next payroll, the exception is rare and small. Roughly KES 14,000 for the whole year, across about 800 requests. That's a budgetable figure, and unlike an open-ended advance book, it doesn't surprise anybody. Our Finance Manager now defends the scheme himself, for exactly the reason you predicted: the forecast impact is a fixed ceiling, known in advance.

*Advances teach people to live on next month's money.* This is the one I'd gently push back on. The loader I mentioned was doing precisely that — with six apps, at interest, in a spiral. Inside our scheme the maximum is 40% of net, repaid at the next payroll, no fee. He can't compound with us. He can compound elsewhere, where we can't see it, where the calls come to reception, and where it ends up as a missed run and a gap on the roster.

**The comparison I'd ask Brenda to put in front of the MD**

A KES 9,000 advance costs us nothing net. It comes back at the next payroll. A missed Mombasa run costs operations, fleet and the depot simultaneously, and none of it sits on one budget line — it lands on three departments and shows up as absence. That comparison is the reason the write-off figure above is the only number I'd defend as a cost of the scheme.

**The policy shape Brenda can propose**

- Cap: 40% of net pay (with the statutory two-thirds deduction check applied to the total, not just to us)
- Frequency: one advance per pay cycle
- Repayment: full, at the next payroll, no fee, no interest
- Approval route: payroll portal, rules-based, decision within the cycle, no discretion at my end
- Annual review of volume, write-offs and absence trends, tabled to Finance

That's the whole document. It's a page of rules, not a banking operation.

**Where I think your advice holds, and where it doesn't**

The version of your advice with a number in it is right. Three months' notice, a financial literacy session and a closed window is a sound answer to "advances are unmanaged" — and we started from exactly that unmanaged position. It's a weak answer to "what happens to our people on the Tuesday their child is sent home from school over fees." SACCO loans take two to three weeks and need guarantors. We pointed people there and the queue was real. Financial literacy is worth running — we still do — but literacy isn't a bridge on a Tuesday afternoon.

What I'd propose isn't that we keep advances informal. It was the informal version that broke, and any Finance Manager is right to be worried about it. It's that we keep them written down, capped and visible. The window closes on the uncontrolled version, not on the emergency itself.

Peter, if your Finance Manager wants the forecast argument settled properly, ours is happy to walk him through it directly. That's the part of your case we're convinced by, and it's the part our Finance Manager now agrees with.

Brenda — you said your Finance Manager is right that some people will take an advance every month, and he's right. That's solvable with a cap and a frequency limit rather than a closure. If it helps, I'm happy to share the policy outline with you directly; it's not proprietary, it's just a page of rules, and you may find it saves you drafting from scratch before the 18th.
